draft.title: Managing coasts
card: Structures built to block or slow the sea. A sea wall is built along the shore to stop waves reaching land. A groyne is a wall built out into the sea to trap sand moving along the beach.
Working with natural processes instead of building a barrier. Beach nourishment adds sand to a beach so waves lose energy on it. Dune replanting uses dune plants, whose roots hold sand in place.
Councils can use rules to keep new buildings back from the shore. This keeps people and property out of the way of erosion and storms.

Each method has costs. A sea wall can be expensive and can leave the beach in front of it worn away. A groyne can leave less sand for the beach further along the coast. Sand added to a beach can be washed away again.
draft.remember: Coasts can be managed by building structures, working with natural processes, or planning where buildings go.

a.q: Which method manages a coast by adding sand so waves lose energy on the beach?
a.why: Beach nourishment puts new sand on a beach so waves lose energy on it. A groyne is tempting because it also deals with sand, but it traps sand that is already moving along the beach instead of adding any.
a.clue: Which method brings in new sand?

b.q: A council in New South Wales builds a groyne to hold sand on a beach in front of a town. What problem might it cause?
opts: Less sand reaching the beach further along the coast
Dune plants being pulled out by the structure
More sand being washed from the beach it protects
Buildings being allowed closer to the shore
b.why: A groyne traps sand moving along the beach, so the beach further along the coast may get less sand. The other options do not follow from trapping sand: a groyne holds sand on the beach it protects, and it does not change planning rules.
b.clue: Think about where the trapped sand would otherwise have gone.

b.best: Less sand reaching the beach further along the coast
